- **The Hebrew Bible:** The source is the *lēv* (heart), not the brain. Examples are Proverbs 4:23 ("from it flow the springs of life") and Genesis 6:5 ("every intention of the thoughts of his heart").
- Genesis 6:5 speaks of "the intention of the thoughts of his heart," and Luke 1:51 of "the thoughts of their hearts."

5. **Transient, yet weighty.** Human thoughts are "but a breath" (Psalm 94:11) and "futile" (1 Corinthians 3:20). Yet God weighs them (Proverbs 15:26), and before the flood they were the measure of human wickedness (Genesis 6:5). God's thoughts, by contrast, are "very deep" (Psalm 92:5), "vast" (Psalm 139:17) and "higher" (Isaiah 55:8–9).
| intention / intent | H3336 *yēṣer* | Gen 8:21 | *yēṣer* is also in Gen 6:5; central to origins |

The *arising* is not commanded, but it is not neutral either. What comes up shows the condition of the heart (Gen 6:5; Mark 7:21). So thoughts that arise reveal the heart, and devising engages the will. The heart itself can be changed from outside: written on, given discretion, guarded, or darkened.

This refines the earlier point. The *capacity* to devise isn't good or evil in itself; it's what artisans and God also do. | **One further citation fix found** | 1 | 2Sa 14:13–14 in 10.7 *Planning* (§3.12) |

**2Sa 14:13–14, in 10.7 *Planning*.** This is a citation fix of the #1990 kind: the same Joab issue in a place the #1987 reading did not list. Replace the paragraph that begins *"A plan can also be held against someone's good"* with:

> A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).

| **10.7 Choosing and setting direction**, new section ***Planning*** | The account of looking ahead. Planning carries a choice ahead (Gen 11:6; Pro 16:9). It covers: weighing first (Luk 14:28–33; Pro 31:15–16; Judg 19:30); planning without knowing (Act 27:10–14, 39–41; Rom 1:13; Jam 4:15); a plan carrying a person's word (2Co 1:17–18); planning together and parting (Act 15:37–39; Luk 23:51–52); planning for another's good (Dan 6:3–4), with the king's planning measured against God's (2Sa 14:13–14); a purpose held (Psa 17:3, 5; Act 11:23; 2Ti 3:10; 1Ch 29:18; Rom 8:6–7; Isa 26:3); devised from one's own heart (1Ki 12:32–33; Neh 6:8); the plan and its outcome (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38–39; Psa 21:11; Dan 11:24; Gen 50:20); seen and disclosed (1Ch 28:9; 1Co 4:3–5) | New section |

verses.text: “And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.

observations.text: In Isa.58.2, Ezra.6.21, and 1Chr.28.9 'seek/worship' sits squarely within the base cultic-consultation/devotion sense of H1875, with no further distinguishing nuance beyond ordinary devotional seeking of God.

M15 (know), M36 (serve), M34 (whole/forever), M47 (heart/mind), M64 (plan), M06 (thought), M30/M59 (forsake), M18 (willing) all co-occur with H1875 in 1Chr.28.9; H1875's own vantage is that the verse pairs two mirrored uses of darash -- human seeking of God and divine searching of the heart -- forming the verse's relational spine that the other M-codes (serving, willing heart, forsaking) orbit as conditions or consequences of that mutual seeking.

1Chr.28.9, Prov.11.27, and Job.39.8 all render darash as 'searches' but span three distinct registers: God searching all hearts (devotional-omniscient), a person searching for evil (moral-negative object), and a wild animal searching for pasture (literal/animal). This triad illustrates the verb's semantic elasticity across divine, moral, and mundane subjects within one surface form.

God's extension of the characteristic (his willingness to be sought/found) is shown as both conditional and responsive: conditional on genuine seeking ('If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever', 1Chr.28.9), yet also shown as gracious and unconditioned in Isa.65.1 ('I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me') -- God's self-disclosure as available to be inquired of exceeds strict conditionality, showing both a covenantal-conditional pattern and a gracious-responsive pattern.

Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside seeking include 'heart/mind' (M47, frequently paired as the seat/manner of seeking, e.g. 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, Ps.119.2/10), 'trust' (M19, Ps.9.10, Isa.31.1), and 'forsake' (M30/M59, as antithetical pairing, Ps.9.10, 1Chr.28.9) -- these co-occur with notable frequency, showing seeking is characteristically bound to heart-language and its antithesis, forsaking.

Seeking consistently PRECEDES finding/being found and its resulting blessings: Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'; Isa.55.6 'Seek the Lord while he may be found'; 1Chr.28.9 'If you seek him, he will be found by you' -- the sequence is invariably seek-then-find, never the reverse, establishing seeking as the necessary antecedent condition.

The seek-then-find sequence is causal-conditional rather than merely correlational or developmental: the finding is explicitly conditioned upon the seeking ('IF you seek him, he WILL be found'), establishing a covenantal cause-and-effect relationship rather than a coincidental temporal succession.
yēṣer ("intention", "inclination") is the same word as the potter's thing formed, and as our frame. The inclination of the heart is itself something formed
God knows the inclination before it acts ("what they are inclined to do even today")

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **Knowing is not enough.** Belshazzar *"knew all this"* and did not humble his heart (Dan 5:22). In the plan set, God *"understands every plan"* (1Ch 28:9). The will set adds that the person's own knowing does not move the will.
- verses not cited in v2 and cited in v3: exactly the 18 above. The other 13 gains add places for verses already cited, such as Deu 18:6, 2Sa 13:28, 1Ch 28:9 and Psa 19:14.

**4. Knowing a thought is separate from producing it.** 1 Corinthians 2:11 says only "the spirit of that person" knows a person's thoughts, and only God's Spirit knows God's. Separately, God searches and knows human thoughts (Psalm 139:23; 1 Chronicles 28:9; Psalm 94:11; 1 Corinthians 3:20), and so does Jesus (Luke 5:22, 6:8, 11:17; Matthew 9:4, 12:25).

file_lines.section: 4. Verses not cited in the narrative
file_lines.text: | Psa 17:3 | H2161 to plan "purposed" | H3820A heart "heart" |

I read the verses as presenting looking ahead as real but bounded, and as morally charged in both directions. The same words are used for a man's resolve to keep his mouth clean (Psa 17:3) and for the wicked plotting on his bed (Psa 36:4).

verses.text: For I hear the whispering of many — terror on every side!— as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life.

observations.text: Meaning: the prophet's word is spoken as a name over a man ("a terror to yourself"). The same words are then whispered by his close friends against him. Implies: in both Jer 20 and Psa 31, the one who hears the whisper answers by turning to the Lord ("But the Lord is with me"; "But I trust in you"). The verses state both answers. In Lamentations it is God who summoned the terrors.

verses.text: Let them be put to shame and dishonor who seek after my life! Let them be turned back and disappointed who devise evil against me!

observations.text: In Esth.6.2, Job.10.6, Ps.24.6, Ps.27.4, Ps.34.14, Ps.35.4, and Ps.37.36 baqash is used in its standard senses (hostile pursuit, investigative search, devotional seeking, seeking peace) with no notable divergence from the base gloss.

Other M-codes present in Ps.35.4: M07 (put to shame/dishonor/disappointed), M47 (life), M15/M64 (devise). Baqash (seek after my life) names the hostile pursuit that the psalmist prays will be met with shame (M07); it is the initiating act to which the shame-outcome responds, but does not modify the shame-terms themselves.
In Ps.35.4, H1245 (seek) is an operation initiated by the psalmist's enemies, directed toward the psalmist's life ('my life') as the target — hostile pursuit.

file_lines.section: 3B.1 Poor and needy have more than one dimension (researcher's observation, 2026-10-15)
file_lines.text: **Note for reading.** In Psa 40:17, 70:5, 86:1 and 109:22, "poor" in "poor and needy" is H6041 *ʿānî*, which is tagged M24 (§5), and "needy" is H0034 (M09). This was checked in `verse_lexical`. These verses therefore sit on both sides of the M09 / M24 line.

| 3. Needy as an expression to get sympathy or help | **Not in these 27, from the poor themselves.** No poor person here speaks. Lazarus "desired to be fed" but says nothing. What appears is another face: **others speak of the poor**, and in John the words of care are a pretext (Joh 12:6). Whether "needy" said by the needy is aimed at help is a matter for the "I am poor and needy" Psalms (Psa 86:1, 70:5, 40:17, 109:22) and Pro 18:23 *"The poor use entreaties"*. |

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **The outcome is not held.** Plans fail or are overruled (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38). Wills are overruled as well: Herod's intention (Act 12), the Romans' wish to free Paul (Act 28:18–19), Paul's wish to enter the theater (Act 19:30). And human will is set under God's: *"it depends not on human will or exertion"* (Rom 9:16); *"not my will, but yours"* (Luk 22:42).
- **H2803** is rendered "meant" in Genesis 50:20 and "plans" in Proverbs 16:9.
- "The heart of man plans his way" (Prov 16:9)

In Gen 50:20 there are two opposite intentions about one event, expressed with the same verb: "you meant evil … God meant it for good." Human plans are real, but "it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand" (Prov 19:21; also Prov 16:9; Ps 33:10–11; Job 5:12).

file_lines.text: - **The outcome is not held.** Plans fail or are overruled (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38). Wills are overruled as well: Herod's intention (Act 12), the Romans' wish to free Paul (Act 28:18–19), Paul's wish to enter the theater (Act 19:30). file_lines.section: 1.4 He also purposes and does not turn back
file_lines.text: **Both are stated.** The verses say he relents (Jer 18:8, 10; 26:3; 36:3) and that he does not relent or turn back (Jer 4:28; Zec 8:14; Heb 6:17). No verse in this set explains how the two stand together, and this account does not.

file_lines.text: - **Turning:** in Jer 18:8, 11; 26:3 and 36:3, the plan is spoken so that a person may hear and turn.
| H2803I | God shaping disaster that he may relent from (Jer 18:8, 11); God's plans for welfare (Jer 29:11); people devising evil (Psa 35:4); Saul's plot (1Sa 18:25); a ship "threatened" (Jon 1:4) |

**God's intentions in Jeremiah are conditional:** *"if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended"* (Jer 18:8; also 26:3, 36:3). His plan is stated so that people may *"Return, every one from his evil way"* (Jer 18:11). observations.text: The bed hosts both deliberate plotting and meditation on God. The same place carries opposite directions
The path: arising → lodging → reckoning → devising → expression (tongue, lips, eyes) → action (hand, feet)

Flow 5: what is devised comes back. The plan returns on the deviser's head (Est 9:25); the schemer is caught in his own scheme (Psa 10:2); disaster is "the fruit of their devices" (Jer 6:19). God answers "devise wickedness" with "I am devising disaster" (Mic 2:1, 3). file_lines.section: 5. No carrying M-code: read by the act (8)
file_lines.text: - **Reading:** the passage names no desire. It gives the acts in order: he saw, he inquired, he sent, he took. The order is the one 10.6 *Coveting* states in Achan's own words (Jos 7:21). Here the sending is done by a king: messengers go and bring her. Micah's woe in 10.6 names this: they covet and take *"because it is in the power of their hand"* (Mic 2:1–2).

- Micah 2 opens with those *"who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds"* (2:1), who *"covet fields and seize them"* (2:2). Then: *"Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, against this family I am devising disaster"* (2:3).

file_lines.section: 3. New — not yet in any chapter
file_lines.text: 1. **The path from thought to deed (§9.3).** Arising (Dan 2:29; Job 4:13; Luk 24:38) → lodging (Jer 4:14) → reckoning (Isa 53:4) → devising (Ps 36:4) → expression through tongue, lips and eyes (Ps 52:2; Pro 16:30) → action through hand and feet (Mic 2:1; Pro 6:18; Isa 59:7). The same path runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Ps 119:59). Commands address the stages from lodging onward. Arising is not commanded, but it shows the state of the heart.

file_lines.section: 3. New — not yet in any chapter
file_lines.text: 3. **Thoughts that arrive, especially at night (§9.1.2–3).** The bed is where thoughts come unbidden (Dan 2:29) and also where people plot on purpose (Ps 36:4; Mic 2:1). The night thoughts are tied to revelation (Dan 2:29–30).

file_lines.text: - **M18 (20 shared verses).** Read or decided in the M18 strand (for example Luk 18:4 carried in 10.12, Mat 1:19 in 10.7 *Willing*, 1Co 14:35 data). None was forwarded to M07.

file_lines.section: 6. Other M-codes in the same verses
file_lines.text: - **There is no section on shame.** The one section with shame in its heading is **10.3 *Remembering in shame*** (Eze 16:63; 20:43). Shame otherwise appears in passing: 10.7 *Shame at the thing chosen* (Isa 1:29; 65:13), Saul's "to your own shame" (1Sa 20:30) in 10.7, Joseph "unwilling to put her to shame" (Mat 1:19) in 10.7, Ephraim "ashamed and confounded" (Jer 31:19) in 13.1, "some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Dan 12:2) in Ch 2, and *In shame* (Php 3:19) in 10.15.

file_lines.section: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family
file_lines.text: - **A resolve reached after weighing, then turned.** *"her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly"* (Mat 1:19). The next verse: *"But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (1:20). The resolve was still being weighed, and God redirected it.

file_lines.section: 1.6 The will that resolves, intends and steers
file_lines.text: - **Joseph.** *"being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (Mat 1:19–20). He was unwilling to shame her, he resolved, and he went on considering. Then God spoke into the considering.

file_lines.section: 2.2 Passages where Scripture itself puts them together
file_lines.text: 7. **Mat 1:19–20.** Unwilling, then resolved, while still considering, then redirected by God.

file_lines.section: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family
file_lines.text: All four have the step gloss "plan". One word, G1013, is rendered "plan" in one verse and "will" in another. And G1014 is rendered "chooses": *"anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22). In Greek, then, willing, choosing and planning are spoken of with one family of words. This is a fact about the words. What it means for the inner being is still to be read verse by verse.

file_lines.section: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family
file_lines.text: All four have the step gloss "plan". One word, G1013, is rendered "plan" in one verse and "will" in another. And G1014 is rendered "chooses": *"anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22). In Greek, then, willing, choosing and planning are spoken of with one family of words. This is a fact about the words. What it means for the inner being is still to be read verse by verse.

2. **Route them under rule 72.** By scan, God's or the Spirit's will (route A) is 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Luk 22:42 (with B); Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9. Job 39:9 is the wild ox (13.4 Nature).

- **The Son chooses:** *"yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father … and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Mat 11:26–27; Luk 10:21–22). The Father's gracious will and the Son's choosing stand together. Luke adds *"he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit"* (10:21).

file_lines.text: **And at Gethsemane:** *"Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done"* (Luk 22:42). This is the one verse in the set where two wills are named side by side and one is given up to the other.

2. **Route them under rule 72.** By scan, God's or the Spirit's will (route A) is 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Luk 22:42 (with B); Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9. Job 39:9 is the wild ox (13.4 Nature).

- **Gethsemane (A and B):** *"Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done." And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in agony he prayed more earnestly* (Luk 22:42–44). Before it: *"Pray that you may not enter into temptation"* (22:40).

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **The outcome is not held.** Plans fail or are overruled (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38). Wills are overruled as well: Herod's intention (Act 12), the Romans' wish to free Paul (Act 28:18–19), Paul's wish to enter the theater (Act 19:30). And human will is set under God's: *"it depends not on human will or exertion"* (Rom 9:16); *"not my will, but yours"* (Luk 22:42).
- **Also B:** Deu 10:10 (Moses' intercession), Deu 29:20 (the self-blessing heart), Dan 4:25 and 4:32 (the king's learning), Dan 5:21, Luk 22:42.

file_lines.section: B.10 Enraged at a word heard; the ruler's fury (faces 5N, 5O, 5P)
file_lines.text: | AG-227 | **When they heard: rage, the body, and killing.** "When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath"; "And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill"; "When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them"; "take care what you are about to do with these men"; "Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him"; "But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven"; "But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him"; "saying that gods made with hands are not gods"; "When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'" | **Setting:** Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luk 4:16–30); the apostles before the council (Act 5:27–40); Stephen's speech (Act 7:54–58); Demetrius and the craftsmen (Act 19:24–29). **Meaning:** in all four the verse says *when they heard*. The rage goes at once into the body: rising up, grinding teeth, stopping ears, rushing, crying out. In three of the four it moves to killing (Luk 4:29; Act 5:33; Act 7:58). In Ephesus the speaker names the trade at risk (19:27). In the council a Pharisee's counsel stops it (5:34–35). **Implies:** extends AN-01 (anger kindled by something perceived) and AG-149 (God hears, unit 4). - **Imputing intent:** the council to the apostles, *"you intend to bring this man's blood upon us"* (Act 5:28). Peter's answer was *"We must obey God rather than men"* (5:29).

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **Imputing intent.** *"you and the Jews intend to rebel"* (Neh 6:6, plan set) and *"you intend to bring this man's blood upon us"* (Act 5:28, will set). In both, an intention is pinned on the other side by those set against them.

file_lines.text: **Open thread OT-62.** Two of these verses are in OT-62 (anger and Will & Resolve, 7 shared verses): 1Sa 20:30 (anger face 3O, "Anger at a rival honoured") and Psa 106:23 (face 2J, "Intercession before God's wrath"). The trigger for OT-62 is "M64 is analysed: read only these anger verses … for how the two operate together". These two are read here with that in view. The other five OT-62 verses (Eze 20:8, Deu 29:20, Zec 8:14, 1Ti 2:8, Act 5:33) are not in the choose set and are not read.
- **OT-62** Anger (M02) and Will & Resolve (M64) (open). Its 7 verses are 1Sa 20:30, 1Ti 2:8, Act 5:33, Deu 29:20, Eze 20:8, Psa 106:23 and Zec 8:14. None of them has an M47 word.

file_lines.section: James 2:5: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith"
file_lines.text: Then: *"But you have dishonored the poor man"* (v6). Choosing against God's choice is a sin: *"if you show partiality, you are committing sin"* (v9).

file_lines.section: 2 Peter 1:10: "be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election"
file_lines.text: Whoever lacks these is described in inner terms: *"so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins"* (v9).

file_lines.section: Revelation 17:14: "those with him are called and chosen and faithful"
file_lines.text: The chapter is a vision of judgment on *"the great prostitute"*, with whom *"the dwellers on earth have become drunk"* (v2). The seer himself is moved: *"When I saw her, I marveled greatly"* (v6). He is asked *"Why do you marvel?"* (v7). Those who marvel at the beast are *"the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world"* (v8). The vision *"calls for a mind with wisdom"* (v9).

file_lines.text: - *dialogismos* is both inner reasoning and outward quarrel or dispute (1Ti 2:8; Php 2:14).

**4. One word covers both inner reasoning and outward dispute.** *Dialogismos* is rendered "thoughts" (Mark 7:21), but also "quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8), "disputing" (Philippians 2:14) and "opinions" (Romans 14:1). The same activity happens inside a person as an inner conversation and between people as argument.

| *dialogizomai / dialogismos* | Honest troubled reasoning · hardened anxious reasoning · inner questioning seen by Jesus · reasoning together into murder · self-talk of the rich man · **quarrel, dispute, opinions** · argument about greatness · futile thinking · evil thoughts from the heart · **partiality: "judges with evil thoughts"** · thoughts revealed by the child set for a sign | Luk 1:29 · Mar 8:16–17; Mat 16:7–8 · Mar 2:6, 8; Luk 5:21–22; 6:8; 9:47 · Luk 20:14; Mat 21:25 · Luk 12:17 · **1Ti 2:8 ("without anger or quarreling"); Phili 2:14; Rom 14:1** · Luk 9:46 · Rom 1:21; 1Co 3:20 · Mar 7:21; Mat 15:19 · Jam 2:4 · Luk 2:35 | **Inner reasoning becomes outward quarrel when it is shared and set on one's own standing** (Luk 9:46; Rom 14:1) (R). file_lines.section: H. The perish words (added in v3)
file_lines.text: 5. **Stated causes of perishing.** Forgetting God and serving other gods (Deu 8:19–20; 30:18; Jos 23:16); not repenting (Luk 13:3, 5); not believing (Jude 5); desires to be rich (1Ti 6:9); "those who are far from you shall perish" (Psa 73:27); taking the sword (Mat 26:52); false witness (Pro 19:9; 21:28). Luk 13:3 and 2Th 2:10 are woven. The rest are carried by the death-in-the-living causes and stay here as sources for when those strands are read.

file_lines.section: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family
file_lines.text: **The epistle openings and requests** (*"I want you to know"*, Phi 1:12; Tit 3:8; Jude 5; 1Ti 2:8; 5:14; 2Jo 12; Phm 13; 3Jo 10) mostly use the word as a stated wish in teaching. Their bearing on setting direction is slight, but each still needs to be read.
